name: West Town Upside
description:
West Town was three neighborhoods pretending to be one: Wicker Park, Bucktown, and Ukrainian Village. Each had its own identity, its own pride, its own argument about where the boundaries were. The incorporation resolved the argument by dissolving all three into a single corporate development zone and renaming it West Town Upside — 'upside' being corporate real estate jargon for unrealized property value. The name stuck because the residents found it grimly appropriate. Everything here has been flipped: community into commodity, culture into content, neighborhood into investment vehicle.

Wicker Park's six-way intersection — the old heart of the neighborhood's indie music, art, and nightlife scene — is now the Hexagon, a corporate entertainment complex operated by an Axiom lifestyle subsidiary. The Hexagon's six streets radiate outward like spokes, each themed to a different 'authentic urban experience': live music (approved), street art (commissioned), vintage shopping (curated), craft dining (algorithmic), nightlife (monitored), and 'community' (a word that has been emptied of meaning and refilled with brand strategy). The Hexagon draws Tier 3-5 visitors from across the Corridor for a night out that feels dangerous without being dangerous, creative without being challenging, and urban without being urban. It is the most profitable entertainment district in the outer Corridor, and the most soulless.

Bucktown's residential streets have been converted to what the developer calls 'Heritage Housing' — pre-collapse homes maintained in original condition on the outside and gutted to corporate specification on the inside. The Ukrainian Village section retains its churches — the golden domes are too photogenic to demolish — but the congregations are gone, replaced by event spaces, corporate retreats, and a neural-interface meditation center called 'Cathedral' that charges by the minute for spirituality optimized to your neurochemical profile.

The soul of old West Town didn't die. It moved to the attics. Literally. The Upside's underground scene operates in the literal upper stories of the Heritage Housing blocks — attic spaces, rooftop additions, the vertical margins that corporate renovation didn't reach. Musicians, artists, designers, and the kinds of creative people who can't afford to live in the neighborhoods they made interesting have colonized the spaces between the corporate floors. They call themselves the Garret, and their work — music, art, fashion, code — is the real thing that the Hexagon's corporate subsidiaries spend millions trying to simulate. The irony sustains them. The rent does not.

sights: The Hexagon intersection blazing with themed entertainment lighting in six directions
Heritage Housing with pre-collapse facades and corporate interiors — the architectural uncanny valley
Ukrainian Village's golden church domes repurposed as corporate event venue branding
Garret artists visible in upper-story windows, creating the culture the ground floors monetize
The contrast between the Hexagon's curated street art and the Garret's actual street art, often on the same wall
Nightlife crowds moving through monitored entertainment corridors — fun under surveillance
sounds: The Hexagon's live music — professional, polished, algorithmically setlisted
Garret music bleeding through Heritage Housing attic windows — raw, unpermitted, alive
The Cathedral's neural-interface meditation tones — synthetic tranquility at premium rates
Nightlife crowd noise — laughter, shouting, the collective sound of people spending money
The specific silence of the Ukrainian churches between corporate events — stone remembering prayer
smells: The Hexagon's curated food scene — each street themed to a different cuisine, all excellent, all corporate
Paint and turpentine from Garret studios — the smell of art made without permission
Old incense in the Ukrainian churches, lingering beneath the corporate event catering
Alcohol — the Upside has the highest density of bars in the outer Corridor, and it smells like it
atmosphere.feel: The Upside feels like watching someone wear your clothes. Everything here was taken from somewhere real, polished, branded, and resold. For people who remember what these neighborhoods were — or for people who create the kind of culture the Hexagon commodifies — the Upside is infuriating. For everyone else, it's a good night out. Both reactions are valid, and the tension between them is the Upside's actual energy source.

demographics: Approximately 85,000 residents. Tier 3-4 in Heritage Housing and the Hexagon's residential towers. Tier 1-2 in the Garret attic spaces and service-worker housing at the margins. The Ukrainian community that gave Ukrainian Village its name is functionally extinct here — a handful of elderly residents remain, and the churches outlived their congregations.
dangers: The Hexagon's surveillance — entertainment districts are monitored with nightclub-level density
Getting identified as Garret-affiliated in a corporate space — the Upside's owners don't appreciate the competition
The nightlife economy attracts predatory behavior — augment theft, credit fraud, neural-interface exploitation
Heritage Housing's corporate security mistaking residents for intruders in their own attic spaces
The emotional damage of watching your culture sold back to you at markup
opportunities: The Garret's creative network — artists, musicians, and designers with skills and connections across the Corridor
The Hexagon as a hunting ground for corporate intelligence, high-value targets, and social engineering
The Ukrainian churches as neutral meeting spaces — corporate event scheduling leaves gaps
Cultural credibility — association with the Garret carries weight in the Counterfeit and the Circuit
Nightlife as cover — the crowds, the noise, the neural-interface distortion make the Upside excellent operational territory
story_hooks: A Garret musician has composed a piece that, when played through neural interfaces, unlocks suppressed memories of pre-incorporation West Town — and the corporate licensee wants it destroyed
The last Ukrainian church congregation is fighting eviction from their own building, and the elder who holds the original property deed needs someone to retrieve it from a corporate archive
Kyle is hired to protect a Garret artist during a covert exhibition in the Hexagon itself — guerrilla culture in the belly of the beast
frequented_by: Tier 3-5 visitors consuming the Hexagon's curated entertainment
Garret artists living in the margins and creating the culture the ground floors sell
Corporate entertainment employees managing the Upside's brand identity
Nightlife operators, promoters, and the people who profit from other people's fun
Kyle, when a job requires the specific social camouflage of a crowded entertainment district
